sm: This LifeNews piece by Mark Tapscott argues that Americans were giving thanks to God long before Abraham Lincoln's 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation. It quotes Lincoln's call to set apart the last Thursday of November as a day of thanksgiving and praise, acknowledging the blessings of the year despite the war and the nation's sins, including slavery. Lincoln's example led every later president to issue a Thanksgiving proclamation. Congress made Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1870 and fixed it on the fourth Thursday of November in 1941. The author says Thanksgiving was never merely a gesture between Native Americans and Puritans, but was widely practiced to the Christian God from the colonial era through the Civil War.

This part traces official thanksgiving proclamations before and during the Revolution. In 1761, Massachusetts Governor Francis Bernard called for thanks to Almighty God, and also thanked the British king. In 1774 the Massachusetts Provincial Congress urged congregations to give thanks for health, good seasons, the gospel and colonial unity. The Continental Congress called a day of humiliation, fasting and prayer on July 20, 1775, and John Adams predicted millions would be on their knees that day. Later appeals followed the 1777 victory at Saratoga, the exposure of Benedict Arnold's treason in 1780, and the 1781 victory at Yorktown. The 1781 call also cited French aid, a plentiful harvest, and the Articles of Confederation.

The final part says the practice continued after the Constitution. In 1789 Representative Elias Boudinot of New Jersey urged that citizens be offered a chance to thank God together, and both chambers asked President Washington to encourage Americans to give God sincere and humble thanks. The author cites historian Paul Johnson on the Second Great Awakening, a long series of revivals from the 1790s nearly to the Civil War. He then quotes Alexis de Tocqueville, who wrote in 1840 that in America the spirit of religion and the spirit of freedom were intimately united. Tocqueville called religion the foremost of the country's political institutions and indispensable to republican institutions. The author concludes that Americans have been a thanksgiving people since before the United States existed.
